questions.q: What is deterministic matching, as defined in this lesson?
options: Matching based on exact rules applied to specific fields — if they match exactly (or after simple standardization), the records are treated as the same entity
Matching based purely on random sampling of records
A method that never produces explainable results
A method that only works on image data
questions.explain: Deterministic matching is rule-based and exact — a defined field match (like an exact tax ID match) decides the outcome, with no scoring involved.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of deterministic matching, per this lesson?
options: It is too slow to run on large datasets
It is brittle — it breaks when there are typos, nicknames, or formatting differences in the fields being compared
It requires a probabilistic model to even run
It cannot be explained to a business user
questions.explain: The lesson states deterministic rules break the moment a field varies slightly — like 'Robert' vs. 'Bob' — making it unreliable as the sole method on free-text fields.

questions.q: How does probabilistic matching combine information from multiple fields?
options: It ignores all but one field entirely
It scores the similarity of each field, weights those scores, and produces one overall confidence that two records are the same entity
It requires every single field to match exactly
It picks a field at random to decide
questions.explain: Probabilistic matching computes weighted, per-field similarity scores and combines them into an overall match confidence, rather than requiring exact agreement.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a probabilistic match process typically uses two thresholds instead of one?
options: Two thresholds are required by law in every industry
A single cutoff either merges too aggressively (false positives) or misses too much (false negatives); the middle band routes uncertain cases to a human steward
Two thresholds make the system run twice as fast
It has no real purpose and is just a convention
questions.explain: The lesson explains the review band is deliberate: forcing every case into match/no-match with one cutoff creates real costs in both directions, so uncertain cases go to a steward instead.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how do most real MDM implementations typically use these two approaches?
options: They use only deterministic matching and never probabilistic matching
They use only probabilistic matching and never deterministic matching
They use deterministic rules to catch the easy, certain cases, with probabilistic scoring layered underneath for everything else
They alternate randomly between the two approaches
questions.explain: The lesson recommends using both together: deterministic matching where a trustworthy unique identifier exists, and probabilistic matching for the larger set of fuzzy, free-text cases.
